artifact.recommendation: Adopt a managed search service behind an internal abstraction and a portable, vendor-neutral index pipeline.
reasoning: It is the only option that credibly meets the four-month launch deadline while delivering faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing.
The managed service already supports all required launch capabilities, whereas the prior internal prototype achieved only basic keyword search after six engineer-weeks.
Building and operating an open-source cluster conflicts with the team's capacity and the prohibition on increasing operational on-call headcount.
Delaying for dedicated hiring risks losing the contracted design-partner expansion because the expected delay exceeds the commercially tolerable window.
Vendor dependence can be bounded through canonical search documents, an internal query/indexing abstraction, and the service's bulk export API.
The projected first-year cost is material but proportionate at 7 percent of the product infrastructure budget, given the staffing and launch constraints.
considerations: Keep the abstraction focused on business-level search operations and avoid attempting to normalize every vendor-specific feature.
Own the canonical document schema, source-of-truth data, indexing pipeline, relevance test corpus, and configuration history outside the vendor.
Validate that bulk export includes all data and metadata needed to rebuild indexes elsewhere; periodically test export and reindex procedures.
Define service-level objectives for indexing latency, query availability, relevance, and recovery before contracting.
Use contract terms covering data portability, price changes, termination assistance, security, privacy, regional hosting, and data deletion.
Schedule a post-launch review using actual traffic, cost, relevance, and operational data to reconsider managed versus self-operated search.
assumptions: The managed service can complete security, privacy, procurement, and integration reviews without jeopardizing the four-month deadline.
Its near-real-time indexing behavior and relevance controls satisfy product requirements at expected scale.
The 7 percent budget estimate includes realistic query, indexing, storage, replication, and data-transfer charges.
The company retains an authoritative copy of source data and can regenerate canonical search documents independently.
The design-partner expansion is sufficiently valuable that avoiding delay outweighs the managed-service premium.
risks: Vendor-specific query semantics or relevance tuning may leak through the abstraction and make migration harder than expected.
Usage growth or pricing changes could make managed-service costs materially exceed the year-one estimate.
A nominal bulk export capability may be too slow, incomplete, expensive, or operationally untested during an urgent migration.
Service limits, outages, or indexing lag could affect the launch experience while the internal team has limited search expertise.
Overengineering portability could consume scarce engineering time and threaten the deadline.
Security or procurement review could become the critical path.
evidence_needed: A benchmark using representative documents and queries confirming relevance, typo tolerance, facet correctness, indexing latency, and p95/p99 query latency.
A detailed total-cost model across base, expected, and high-growth scenarios, including overages and data transfer.
A timed migration drill that exports data and rebuilds a functional index in an alternative engine from canonical documents.
Documentation of API limits, export guarantees, disaster recovery, availability commitments, and termination procedures.
Security, privacy, compliance, and data-residency review results.
A delivery plan showing integration, testing, relevance tuning, procurement, and contingency milestones within four months.

artifact.recommendation: Adopt a managed search service behind an internal abstraction and a portable, vendor-neutral index pipeline.
reasoning: It is the only option that credibly meets the four-month launch deadline while providing faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing at launch.

Building immediately is inconsistent with current staffing: the prior prototype consumed six engineer-weeks without delivering key features, while production operations would add on-call and upgrade duties that existing constraints prohibit.
Delaying for dedicated hires would threaten the contracted design-partner expansion and is unnecessary because search relevance is important but not a core differentiator.
The projected year-one cost is proportionate at 7 percent of the infrastructure budget.
Lock-in can be materially reduced by generating canonical search documents, isolating vendor-specific APIs behind an internal adapter, and retaining a tested bulk-export and reindex path.
considerations: Define the abstraction around business search capabilities rather than attempting to normalize every vendor feature.
Keep the canonical document schema and indexing event stream vendor-neutral and independently retained.
Automate full reindexing from the system of record; treat vendor export as a supplementary migration mechanism, not the only exit path.
Set relevance, indexing-latency, availability, and cost thresholds before contracting, with alerts and periodic reviews.
Run a migration drill before renewal or major vendor-specific feature adoption to verify that portability remains practical.
assumptions: The managed service's documented features satisfy production-scale requirements, not merely prototype use cases.
Its near-real-time indexing latency and availability meet product expectations.
The year-one cost projection includes expected query volume, indexing, storage, replicas, support, and data-transfer charges.
Contracting, security, privacy, and procurement reviews can complete within the four-month window.
The canonical search document can represent all required facets and relevance inputs without relying on an irreducibly vendor-specific source model.
risks: Vendor-specific ranking configuration, analytics, synonyms, or query syntax may leak through the abstraction and increase switching cost.
Traffic or index growth could make managed-service pricing materially higher than forecast.
Export throughput, format, quotas, or fees may make migration slower than the existence of an export API implies.
Service outages, regional limitations, or indexing lag could affect the product without an internal operations team able to remediate the platform directly.
An overly broad abstraction could slow feature delivery while still failing to provide genuine portability.
evidence_needed: A production-scale proof of concept measuring relevance, typo handling, facet correctness, indexing latency, query latency, and failure behavior.
A complete three-year cost model with sensitivity analysis for traffic, document size, replicas, analytics, support, and egress.
Export and full-reindex benchmarks showing time, cost, format fidelity, rate limits, and recovery procedures.
Contract review covering data ownership, deletion, portability, price-change protections, service levels, and termination assistance.
A staffing estimate for integration, relevance tuning, monitoring, incident response, and migration maintenance.
Validation that an alternative engine can ingest the canonical documents and serve a representative query suite with acceptable adaptation effort.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses the deadline, staffing, required capabilities, and migration-path constraints.
The reasoning is traceable to the supplied evidence, with citations covering nearly every decisive claim.
The report recognizes that portability requires more than an API wrapper and proposes canonical documents, independently retained source data, reindexing, and migration drills.
It appropriately treats vendor export as something to validate rather than proof of an adequate exit path.
The assumptions, risks, and evidence-needed sections clearly distinguish known facts from items requiring validation.
It warns that an overbroad abstraction could consume scarce capacity and recommends a business-level interface instead.
It calls for production-scale capability benchmarks, cost sensitivity analysis, contractual protections, and operational objectives before commitment.
weaknesses: The conclusion that managed search is the only credible four-month option is stronger than the evidence establishes; no delivery estimates are supplied for managed integration or a constrained open-source implementation.
The reports do not rank acceptance criteria or specify go/no-go thresholds for procurement completion, benchmark results, cost, migration time, or relevance quality.
The commercial argument relies on loss of a design-partner expansion without quantifying its value relative to vendor cost and switching risk.
The 7 percent cost figure is characterized as proportionate or material without a benchmark, absolute amount, multi-year projection, or approved budget threshold.
The internal abstraction is described conceptually but not scoped enough to estimate its implementation cost within the deadline.
The two visible research artifacts are highly duplicative and provide little independent challenge or option-specific analysis.
unsupported: That managed search is the only option capable of meeting the four-month deadline.
That delaying for hiring is unnecessary because search is not a core differentiator; non-core status supports buying but does not establish that hiring or delay is unnecessary.
That 7 percent of infrastructure budget is proportionate or represents an acceptable managed-service premium.
That vendor dependence can be materially bounded by the proposed controls before export performance and alternative-engine compatibility are tested.
That the expected delay for hiring necessarily reaches the six-month delay referenced in the evidence.

That existing staffing constraints prohibit all self-operated approaches; the evidence says they require on-call ownership, while the constraint prohibits increasing headcount, not explicitly reallocating existing staff.
missing: A weighted comparison of all three options against launch time, feature fit, staffing, operational burden, cost, lock-in, and commercial impact.
A four-month critical-path plan with staffing allocations, procurement deadlines, integration milestones, relevance tuning, contingency time, and an explicit fallback decision date.
Quantified product requirements for corpus size, update rate, query load, latency, availability, recovery objectives, typo behavior, facet accuracy, and relevance quality.
A concrete exit target such as maximum migration duration, acceptable feature degradation, estimated engineering effort, and tested alternative engine.
An analysis of ongoing internal ownership even with managed search, including relevance tuning, schema evolution, monitoring, incidents, and adapter maintenance.
Vendor viability, support quality, regional availability, security posture, compliance requirements, and contractual service remedies.
A comparison of rebuilding from the authoritative source versus bulk export, including which metadata or vendor-managed configuration cannot be regenerated.
Quantification of the design-partner expansion value and the probability that each option causes delay or loss.
A contingency if security or procurement cannot finish in time, or if the proof of concept fails acceptance criteria.
incorrect_assumptions: The report appears to equate a prohibition on increasing on-call headcount with an absolute inability to assign existing staff to on-call rotation.
It assumes the six-month commercial-delay evidence applies directly to the dedicated-hiring option, although no hiring timeline is provided.
It assumes a canonical document can preserve practical portability for ranking behavior, synonyms, analytics, query semantics, and configuration; documents alone do not capture all search behavior.
It assumes successful managed-service feature support implies feasible integration and tuning within four months, pending the reviews and benchmarks it separately identifies.
It implicitly treats year-one cost as sufficient for the buy decision despite lock-in and pricing exposure being inherently multi-year concerns.
critical_risks: There are two visible research reports despite the instruction referring to a single target, so the review target is ambiguous; this assessment treats their substantively shared recommendation as the target.
A procurement, security, privacy, or integration delay could invalidate the central schedule advantage and leave no defined fallback.
The proposed portability layer could either be too thin to prevent lock-in or too broad to meet the launch deadline.
Untested export throughput and incomplete portability of relevance configuration could make emergency migration impractical.
Costs may rise sharply with traffic, document size, replicas, analytics, support, and egress after product dependence is established.
Limited internal search expertise remains an operational and product-quality risk even when infrastructure is managed.
recommended_changes: Replace the categorical recommendation with a conditional decision: select managed search only if dated procurement, benchmark, security, cost, and portability gates pass.
Add a decision matrix scoring all options against each constraint and clearly distinguish observed evidence, estimates, and judgments.
Define measurable acceptance thresholds for relevance, typo tolerance, facet correctness, p95/p99 latency, indexing delay, availability, cost, and migration duration.
Provide a staffed four-month delivery plan and reserve a decision point early enough to execute a fallback.
Quantify the design-partner expansion value and compare expected commercial loss, including probabilities, against three-year total cost and switching exposure.
Specify the minimum viable abstraction and explicitly list vendor-specific capabilities that may remain exposed.
Test full regeneration from the authoritative source and migration to at least one alternative engine; do not rely primarily on bulk export.
Clarify whether existing personnel may be reassigned to on-call and estimate opportunity costs for both managed and self-operated options.
Consolidate the duplicative reports or make their analytical roles distinct, such as recommendation versus adversarial challenge.

strengths: The recommendation directly addresses the launch deadline, required capabilities, staffing limits, and migration constraint.
Reasoning is consistently tied to the supplied evidence, with accurate artifact locators and clear separation of assumptions, risks, and evidence gaps.
The portability strategy is pragmatic: retain source data and canonical documents, isolate vendor APIs, and test full reindexing rather than relying solely on export.
The reports identify major implementation risks, including abstraction leakage, cost growth, export limitations, outages, procurement delays, and overengineering.
Proposed validation covers relevance, facets, typo handling, latency, cost, security, contracts, and migration feasibility.
weaknesses: The conclusion is more confident than the evidence warrants; key feasibility, procurement, scale, cost, and migration questions remain unvalidated.
The alternatives are evaluated asymmetrically: managed search receives a mitigation plan, while no scoped build or hybrid implementation is estimated.
The reports do not define decision thresholds for acceptable relevance, latency, availability, migration time, cost, or adaptation effort.
The evidence does not identify the managed service, deployment model, expected scale, regulatory environment, or alternative migration target.
The two reports largely duplicate one another rather than adding independent analysis.
unsupported: Calling managed search the only option that can credibly meet the four-month deadline is plausible but not established by comparative delivery estimates.
The claim that self-operation conflicts with or is prohibited by the on-call constraint conflates unchanged headcount with inability to assign additional duties.
The delay option is assumed to cause a six-month delay, although the option itself gives no hiring timeline and evidence e5 only describes the consequence of a six-month delay.
Describing 7 percent of the infrastructure budget as proportionate or a managed-service premium requires business-value and alternative-cost comparisons not supplied.
The claim that delaying is unnecessary because search is not a core differentiator is a strategic judgment, not a consequence of the cited evidence.
A documented bulk export API and canonical document format do not by themselves establish a practical migration path.
missing: A milestone-level four-month delivery plan including procurement, security review, integration, relevance tuning, load testing, and contingency time.
Representative production-scale benchmarks and explicit acceptance criteria.
A multi-year total-cost comparison including internal labor, support, overages, egress, replicas, growth, and migration maintenance.
Quantification of the design-partner expansion's value and probability relative to managed-service costs and risks.
A concrete incident-ownership model showing how the capacity-constrained backend team will handle integration, relevance, monitoring, and vendor escalations without new on-call headcount.
Validation against at least one alternative engine, including unsupported schema, query, ranking, synonym, analytics, and facet semantics.
Assessment of security, privacy, compliance, residency, retention, deletion, and contractual requirements.
A fallback plan if procurement or the proof of concept fails early enough to protect the launch.
incorrect_assumptions: Additional search operational duties necessarily require increased on-call headcount rather than reassignment or vendor-supported coverage.
Hiring dedicated engineers necessarily delays launch by six months.
All migration-critical state can be reconstructed from canonical documents or recovered through bulk export; relevance configuration, synonyms, analytics, and operational metadata may not transfer.
The first-year 7 percent estimate is meaningful without validating its inclusions, uncertainty, growth sensitivity, or comparison baseline.
An internal abstraction materially limits lock-in unless an alternative implementation and representative query suite are actually exercised.
critical_risks: The four-month launch may still fail if procurement, security review, integration, or relevance tuning becomes the critical path.
Nominal portability may prove illusory under urgent migration because of proprietary ranking behavior, missing metadata, export limits, or slow reindexing.
Costs may rise sharply with traffic, index growth, replicas, analytics, support, or data transfer.
Limited internal search expertise could impair relevance tuning and incident response even when infrastructure operations are managed.
Building an overly broad abstraction could consume deadline capacity without producing a usable exit path.
recommended_changes: Make the recommendation conditional on a time-boxed proof of concept, completed procurement/security review, and validated cost and migration thresholds.
Replace absolute statements such as “only option” and “constraints prohibit” with evidence-calibrated language.
Provide comparative estimates for all options, including delivery time, staffing, operational burden, cost, and commercial impact.
Define measurable go/no-go criteria for relevance, typo handling, facet correctness, indexing latency, p95/p99 query latency, availability, cost, and migration duration.
Prioritize reproducible reindexing from independently retained source data; treat vendor export as recovery for vendor-held state and verify exactly what it contains.
Test the abstraction by implementing a thin adapter or migration spike against a second engine before committing deeply to proprietary features.
Add milestone checkpoints and a launch contingency if contracting or technical validation misses its deadline.
Lower the reported confidence until the listed evidence is obtained; the current 0.96–0.97 values understate material unresolved uncertainty.

attacks: The managed-service recommendation is directionally plausible but presented as settled before its central schedule advantage has been demonstrated; procurement, security review, integration, tuning, and load testing could consume the four-month window.

The analysis is asymmetric: it develops mitigations for managed search but provides no time-boxed estimate for a minimally scoped open-source or hybrid alternative, so “only credible option” is not established.

The staffing argument conflates fixed on-call headcount with inability to reassign existing personnel. Reassignment may be undesirable, but its opportunity cost has not been compared with managed-service integration and incident ownership.

The portability proposal may create false confidence. Canonical documents and API adapters preserve data shape, not ranking behavior, synonyms, query semantics, analytics, configuration, or operational state.
A documented export API is weak evidence of an executable exit path; throughput, quotas, fees, format fidelity, configuration coverage, and rebuild duration are unknown.
Calling 7 percent of the infrastructure budget proportionate is unsupported without an absolute amount, approved threshold, alternative cost baseline, growth sensitivity, or multi-year projection.

The commercial case improperly maps evidence about the consequence of a six-month delay onto the hiring option without evidence that hiring would take six months or that managed adoption avoids comparable delay risk.

Managed infrastructure does not eliminate internal search ownership. A capacity-constrained team must still handle schemas, relevance, monitoring, incidents, vendor escalation, and adapter maintenance.
The proposed abstraction can fail in either direction: too thin to reduce lock-in or broad enough to delay launch and suppress useful vendor capabilities.
The 0.96–0.97 confidence levels are incompatible with unresolved feasibility, procurement, cost, operational ownership, and migration questions.
falsifiers: Managed search should be rejected as the launch plan if procurement, security, privacy, or residency approval cannot complete by a dated checkpoint that preserves fallback time.

The recommendation is falsified if a representative proof of concept misses predefined thresholds for relevance, typo handling, facet correctness, indexing delay, p95/p99 latency, availability, or failure recovery.
The claimed cost advantage is falsified if a three-year sensitivity model shows expected or high-growth spend exceeding the approved threshold or a fully loaded self-operated alternative.

The claimed practical migration path is falsified if a second engine cannot reproduce the representative query suite from retained source data within an agreed engineering-effort, duration, cost, and feature-degradation limit.

Reliance on export is falsified if a timed drill reveals missing ranking configuration, synonyms, analytics, metadata, excessive fees, restrictive quotas, or rebuild time beyond the recovery objective.
The schedule claim is falsified if a staffed critical-path plan cannot fit contracting, integration, tuning, testing, observability, and contingency into four months.
The staffing rationale is falsified if managed adoption requires comparable backend allocation or on-call burden to a constrained self-operated deployment.
The commercial rationale is falsified if the design-partner expansion’s probability-weighted value does not exceed the managed premium, switching exposure, and launch-failure risk.
The “only credible option” claim is falsified if a scoped alternative can meet launch requirements within four months under the same staffing and acceptance criteria.
evidence_gaps: Named vendor, deployment model, service limits, regional availability, support model, and contractual service remedies.
Quantified corpus size, update rate, query load, growth assumptions, latency targets, availability target, recovery objectives, and relevance-quality threshold.
A milestone-level four-month plan with named staffing allocations, procurement deadlines, contingency reserve, fallback trigger, and accountable owners.
Production-scale benchmark results using representative documents, queries, misspellings, facets, updates, and failure scenarios.
Three-year total-cost comparison including internal labor, support, replicas, analytics, overages, storage, egress, price changes, and migration maintenance.
An explicit incident-ownership model showing how current staff absorb relevance, monitoring, integration, and vendor-escalation work.
A tested second-engine adapter and measured migration drill covering documents, schemas, ranking rules, synonyms, facets, query semantics, analytics, and configuration.
Exact export guarantees covering completeness, format, throughput, quotas, cost, retention, deletion, and termination access.
Quantified value and probability of the design-partner expansion, plus delay probabilities for every option.
Comparative delivery and operating estimates for all three options under identical acceptance criteria.
Security, privacy, compliance, residency, retention, and procurement outcomes.
Evidence that the minimum viable abstraction can be implemented without threatening launch and a list of intentionally nonportable vendor features.

accepted_criticisms: The claim that managed search is the “only credible” four-month option is not established without comparable, time-boxed delivery estimates for managed, open-source, and hybrid approaches.
The managed-service schedule advantage remains conditional on procurement, security, privacy, integration, relevance tuning, and load testing fitting within four months.
The staffing analysis overstates the on-call constraint: unchanged headcount does not prove existing staff cannot be reassigned, and opportunity costs were not compared.
The six-month-delay consequence was applied too directly to hiring without evidence that hiring would actually delay launch by six months.
Calling 7 percent of infrastructure budget proportionate is unsupported without absolute cost, thresholds, alternatives, growth sensitivity, and a multi-year model.
Managed infrastructure still requires internal ownership of schemas, relevance, monitoring, incidents, escalation, and adapter maintenance.
A practical migration path has not been demonstrated until configuration portability, rebuild duration, cost, feature degradation, and a second-engine adapter are tested.
The proposed abstraction could be too thin to reduce lock-in or too broad to fit the launch schedule.
Confidence of 0.96–0.97 is too high given unresolved feasibility, procurement, cost, ownership, and migration questions.
rejected_criticisms: The report assumed canonical documents preserve ranking behavior, synonyms, analytics, query semantics, and operational state. It explicitly warned that these may remain vendor-specific and called for configuration retention, representative-query testing, and migration drills.

The report treated a documented export API as sufficient proof of an executable exit path. It explicitly identified throughput, completeness, fees, quotas, metadata, and rebuild performance as validation gaps.

The core preference for managed search is unsupported. The visible evidence still favors it: required features already exist, the prior build prototype fell well short after six engineer-weeks, self-operation adds recurring on-call and upgrade work, and the team is already at capacity.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Provisionally select managed search behind a minimal business-level adapter and independently retained canonical indexing pipeline, but commit only if early, dated gates confirm procurement/security completion, representative performance and relevance, acceptable three-year cost, sustainable internal ownership, and a tested regeneration or second-engine migration path. In parallel, produce a comparable scoped fallback estimate; abandon the managed launch plan if any critical gate misses the checkpoint needed to preserve fallback time.
reasons: Managed search remains the best-supported option on the visible evidence, so the recommendation’s direction was correct.
The original categorical wording and very high confidence exceeded what the evidence could support.
Conditional gates directly address the unresolved schedule, cost, operational, and portability risks.
Comparative estimates are necessary before claiming that no open-source or hybrid fallback can meet the same acceptance criteria.
Portability should rely primarily on reproducible rebuilding from authoritative retained data, with vendor export treated as a separately tested recovery mechanism.

accepted_criticisms: The claim that managed search is the “only credible option” is not established without comparable, time-boxed delivery estimates for managed, open-source, and hybrid approaches.
The four-month advantage remains conditional on procurement, security, integration, tuning, load testing, and observability fitting a staffed critical path.
The staffing analysis incorrectly treated fixed on-call headcount as proof that existing personnel cannot be reassigned; opportunity costs must be compared across options.
Canonical documents and adapters reduce data-model coupling but do not preserve ranking behavior, synonyms, query semantics, analytics, configuration, or operational state.
A documented bulk export API does not establish a practical exit path without testing completeness, throughput, quotas, fees, fidelity, and rebuild duration.
Calling 7 percent of the infrastructure budget proportionate is unsupported without absolute cost, approved thresholds, alternatives, growth sensitivity, and multi-year total cost.
The six-month-delay consequence was applied too directly to hiring despite no evidence establishing a six-month hiring timeline.
Managed infrastructure still requires internal ownership of schemas, relevance, monitoring, incidents, escalation, and adapter maintenance.
The abstraction must be narrowly scoped because it could otherwise be too thin to provide portability or too broad to meet the deadline.
Confidence of 0.96–0.97 is too high given unresolved schedule, procurement, cost, operating-model, and migration feasibility.
The recommendation should include measurable, dated go/no-go gates and an early fallback decision point.
rejected_criticisms: The evidence does not justify rejecting managed search as the leading candidate: it already supplies the required features, while the prototype and self-operation evidence indicate materially higher delivery and operational risk.
Canonical documents and an independently retained source of truth remain valuable portability controls; the criticism limits their scope but does not invalidate them.
The design-partner evidence remains relevant to urgency even though it does not prove the hiring option would cause exactly six months of delay.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Treat managed search as the leading but conditional launch plan, not a settled or uniquely credible choice. Commit only if an early, time-boxed proof of concept meets defined relevance, facet, typo-handling, indexing-latency, query-latency, availability, cost, security, procurement, staffing, and migration thresholds. In parallel, estimate a minimally scoped self-operated or hybrid fallback under identical criteria, define a dated fallback trigger, retain authoritative source data and canonical documents, keep the adapter minimal, and validate reindexing into a second engine rather than relying on bulk export alone.
reasons: Managed search has the strongest visible feature-fit evidence and avoids the known cluster on-call and upgrade burden.
The prior prototype’s limited result after six engineer-weeks makes an immediate internal build comparatively risky, but it does not quantify every possible scoped alternative.
The central schedule claim is still an assumption because no milestone-level managed-service plan or procurement outcome is provided.
Portability is plausible only as a tested regeneration and adaptation capability; data-shape portability alone is insufficient.
Neither the 7 percent first-year cost nor the commercial value of avoiding delay is adequate for a multi-year economic conclusion.
A conditional recommendation preserves the evidence-supported direction while matching confidence to the unresolved feasibility questions.

artifact.decision: Provisionally select managed search as the leading launch plan, subject to early go/no-go gates and a concurrently estimated fallback; the evidence does not justify treating it as settled or uniquely credible.
artifact.action: Run a time-boxed managed-service proof of concept and procurement/security review, define measurable acceptance thresholds, build a staffed four-month critical path, compare three-year costs and internal ownership across options, and test regeneration into a second engine. Commit only if all critical gates pass before a dated fallback trigger.
reasons: Managed search has the strongest demonstrated feature fit: it already supports faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing.
The internal prototype delivered only basic keyword search after six engineer-weeks, making an immediate internal build comparatively risky.
Self-operation adds recurring on-call ownership and quarterly upgrades while the backend team is already at capacity.
Managed service reduces infrastructure operations but does not remove internal responsibility for integration, relevance, monitoring, incidents, and migration controls.
The four-month advantage remains unproven because procurement, security, integration, tuning, load testing, and contingency have not been placed on a staffed schedule.
Canonical documents and an adapter reduce coupling, but practical portability requires a measured rebuild into another engine.
Year-one cost and commercial urgency support investigation, but neither establishes a complete economic case.
evidence: Problem e1: the prior prototype consumed six engineer-weeks and still lacked typo tolerance and faceting.
Problem e2: the managed service supports every required launch feature and documents a bulk export API.
Problem e3: projected managed-service spend at year-one traffic is 7 percent of the product infrastructure budget.
Problem e4: operating the open-source cluster is estimated to require rotating primary on-call ownership and quarterly upgrades.
Problem e5: a six-month launch delay would forgo a contracted design-partner expansion.
Problem e6: the data model can emit vendor-neutral canonical search documents.
The problem requires launch within four months, forbids increasing operational on-call headcount this year, and requires a practical vendor exit path.
Both reviews and the challenge consistently identify missing comparative estimates, acceptance thresholds, procurement outcomes, cost sensitivity, ownership planning, and migration testing.
Both rebuttals converge on managed search as a conditional leader with an early fallback trigger, at substantially reduced confidence.
rejected_alternatives: Build and operate open-source search immediately: not rejected permanently, but presently weaker because the prototype gap, recurring operational burden, and capacity constraint create material schedule risk; it should be estimated as a scoped fallback under identical criteria.

Delay until dedicated search engineers can be hired: presently weakest because it does not address the four-month deadline and exposes the design-partner expansion, although the artifacts do not establish that hiring necessarily entails a six-month delay.
Unconditional managed-service commitment: rejected because schedule, procurement, production performance, total cost, staffing, and migration feasibility remain unvalidated.
Relying on bulk export as the primary exit plan: rejected because documented existence does not establish completeness, throughput, cost, configuration coverage, or recovery duration.
Building a comprehensive vendor-neutral abstraction before launch: rejected because its scope could threaten the deadline without guaranteeing behavioral portability.
minority: Rebuttal-1 says the original position was correct before modification, while rebuttal-2 says it was not; this reflects disagreement about whether an overconfident categorical recommendation counts as substantively correct.

The original research reports assign 0.96–0.97 confidence and call managed search the only credible option, but the challenge, reviews, and both rebuttals support materially lower confidence and conditional language.

assumptions: The supplied problem evidence is accurate but has not been independently benchmarked beyond the visible artifacts.
The authoritative product data remains available independently of the managed service.
A fallback can still protect the launch if its trigger is defined and exercised early.
Managed service lowers platform-operational burden relative to self-operation, though it does not eliminate product and incident ownership.

change_conditions: Reject managed search if procurement, security, privacy, residency, or contracting misses the checkpoint required to preserve fallback time.
Reject or redesign it if the proof of concept misses predefined relevance, correctness, indexing, latency, availability, or recovery thresholds.
Prefer a scoped open-source or hybrid plan if it meets identical launch and staffing criteria with lower total risk or cost.
Reject the economic case if three-year expected or high-growth spend exceeds the approved threshold or fully loaded alternative cost without compensating commercial value.
Reject the claimed migration path if a second-engine drill exceeds agreed effort, duration, cost, or feature-degradation limits.
Reconsider delaying for hiring if launch timing can be preserved or the value of a better internally owned search capability exceeds the design-partner and delay costs.

Define corpus size, update and query rates, growth cases, relevance criteria, facet correctness, indexing-delay targets, p95/p99 latency, availability, and recovery objectives.

artifact.decision: Provisionally choose the managed search service, but treat it as the leading candidate rather than a settled or uniquely credible solution.
artifact.action: Immediately run a time-boxed managed-service proof of concept and parallel fallback estimate. Commit only after dated gates confirm procurement and security timing, representative feature and performance results, sustainable ownership, acceptable three-year cost, and a tested second-engine rebuild path. Keep the adapter minimal, retain authoritative source data and canonical documents independently, and define an early fallback trigger.
reasons: Managed search has the strongest demonstrated launch feature fit: the service supports faceting, typo tolerance, and near-real-time indexing, while the internal prototype delivered only basic keyword search after six engineer-weeks.
Self-operation introduces recurring primary on-call ownership and quarterly upgrades when the backend team is already at capacity and on-call headcount cannot increase.
Waiting to hire creates material schedule and commercial risk, although the artifacts do not establish that hiring would necessarily cause a six-month delay.
The four-month advantage remains unproven until procurement, security, integration, tuning, observability, and load testing are placed on a staffed critical path.

Canonical documents and an adapter reduce data-model and API coupling, but practical portability requires testing ranking, query semantics, configuration, synonyms, facets, and rebuild duration in another engine.
The year-one seven-percent budget figure is insufficient to establish economic acceptability without absolute cost, comparison baselines, growth sensitivity, and a multi-year model.

rejected_alternatives: Do not immediately commit to a self-operated open-source cluster: the available prototype and operations evidence indicate higher delivery and recurring staffing risk, and no scoped plan demonstrates compliance with the four-month and on-call constraints.
